utterances.text: You are claiming that Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was admitted in the United Nations. What's the name of that state today? I think it's called Bosnia-Herzegovina, period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not going to argue with you. My question to you was quite clear. I asked you to tell the Judges if you think -- if it's your -- if you believe that these were equally legitimate parallel structures, please tell the Chamber when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the HZ HB some might call it, was admitted as a member state of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to the manner in which the question is phrased because we are talking about notorious things, about common knowledge. So the Prosecutor, by asking this question, is merely pulling the leg of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I must join -- thank you, Your Honours. I think that the Prosecutor is doing something that is even worse than that. He has his political beliefs which he is defending, and we are quite clear about it. Whose policy he's defending, whose political views he is defending. This is not cross-examination, this is defence of his political views. And he's trying to provoke a discussion with the witness. This is not cross-examination. I will certainly not be allowed to conduct my cross-examination in this way, Your Honours. I'm quite sure about that. You would have interrupted me a long time ago. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, I think Mr. Seric has said it's common knowledge. Are we going to pursue this --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I can rephrase the question, of course, and I agree with that. I do have respond ever see briefly to comments by Mr. Krsnik. I don't submit with respect to the Chamber in the past 12 months I don't believe I've stated a personal political view in this courtroom. I object to that very much. To make the record very, very clear, I was -- I am appointed by the Secretary-General of the United Nations to represent the international community in the investigation and Prosecution of war crimes in the former Yugoslavia, and I do that without bias or prejudice to any party to those conflicts, and I object to these attacks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you know, and it's true, isn't it, that contrary to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Herceg-Bosna was never recognised as a state by the European Community or by the United Nations? True?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, Mr. Prosecutor, but you have already said that you are obviously a representative of one of the parties to the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, as you define it, sir, yes. I represent the international community. And your position is clear --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, your position is clear, and I think the Judges understand it, you blame the international community for the war. And you're correct, I represent the international community. But let's please move on. Now, the --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everybody will be called to account for the sins he committed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The Territorial Defence -- this goes back to the point we were talking about some minutes ago. The Territorial Defence that existed under the former Yugoslavia as a whole, as part of the overall military structure of that state, was abolished by President Izetbegovic on the 8th of April, 1992, and the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established in its place; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't really say it was correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, can the usher please assist us in showing the witness Exhibit P122.1.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to add --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm told that it's --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- regarding the Territorial Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, witness, if you want to add something, you're allowed to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the Territorial Defence. You have a very nice testimony by two officers of the BH Army, Stjepan Siber and Hasan Efendic, who both describe how the Territorial Defence was renamed and how the republican staff of the army -- of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina became the staff of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is one and the same institution, in the same place with only its name changed, and the chief individual who escaped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you can ask you to look at Exhibit 122.1, since you're an historian. Do you have any reason to disagree that this is a true copy of the regulation issued by President Izetbegovic on the 8th of April, 1992 in Sarajevo, establishing the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, isn't it true, sir, that it was only about two days after this that it was Mate Boban, on behalf of the so-called Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna that declared in fact that he did not recognise the Territorial Defence than the only legal military forces on the territory claimed by Herceg-Bosna was the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I'll ask the usher to move us along. I'll ask the usher to put before you Exhibit P123.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand why you use the expression "so-called." And I also think that it was on that same day that Mate Boban issued his communication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Directing your attention, sir, to Exhibit P123, to the third paragraph starting on the first page. Mr. Boban says -- goes on to say: "The Croatian people formed their own defence forces. The Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna has decided that the Croatian Defence Council will have exclusive Supreme Command of these forces. This body is the only legal one, and its name is the only official one." And skipping a paragraph and going to the bottom or the last paragraph: "Did not Mr. Boban say all military formations on the territory of the HZ of Herceg-Bosna are either illegal or enemy formations?"

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what Mr. Boban says. The communication is authentic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he refused and Herceg-Bosna refused to recognise the legality of the armed forces of the state declared to exist by -- or recognised to exist by the European Community and the United Nations; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At page 13 of your report, sir, you claim that an order issued by Bozo Rajic in January 1993, if I read your report correctly, was an effort to solve the parallel structure's problem? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if the witness could be -- perhaps it would be easier if I can -- put the next four -- P214, P215, and P223.2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, directing your attention first of all to Exhibit P214. Is this an order or -- decision, excuse me, issued by the president of the HVO, Jadranko Prlic on the 15th of January, 1993, to declare or execute this issue -- excuse me, the solution to the parallel structure's problem, as you describe it? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, basically the text is the same. I mentioned -- I quoted the text of the 16th of January, but I quoted it quite clearly, and basically they are the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Exhibit P215, if you will, working down the chain of command from the HVO president to the HVO Minister of Defence, this was a similar order issued by Bruno Stojic, the Minister of Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, again, sir, this is a part of your report that wasn't completely clear to me. Were you attempting to suggest that this was an agreed situation, that both the Bosnian Croat side and the Muslim or, to use your term if it assists you, the Presidency side agreed to this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. situation?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there was an agreement or that they agreed with this solution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the truth of the matter is, is it not, this was a unilateral declaration by the HVO side, which in fact was not agreed to and never agreed to by the Muslim side; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not reach an agreement as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We seem to have agreement on that, but so the record is clear, if you would please look at Exhibit 223.2. Did not President Izetbegovic on the 19th of January, 1993, make it very clear that that proposition was rejected?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although I must admit this is the first time that I see this. Mr. Izetbegovic, who, as far as I know, was not supposed to be the president of the Presidency at the time, signed this order, that is, this decision. You know that his term of office expired sometime before this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to change topics a bit, and I noticed at the last break and I apologise, I think we stopped at an hour instead of an hour and is a minutes. For some reason I had 2.00 stuck in my head, and when I counted off an hour and 15, it brought us to 3.15. I'm sorry, my mistake. I don't know what are pleasure is at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll make a break right now. We will resume at 5.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott. At 7.00, some of the Judges will have some meetings, so we will make an earlier recess, about 15 minutes earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, before moving to another topic, just one final point. You said at page 12 of your report that attempts at cooperation, and you were making reference to the Croats on the one side and the Muslims or Bosniaks on the other side, and you said at page 12: "Attempts at cooperation were insincere on both sides"; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. I need to find the sentence. Could you tell me -- could you give me some indication, perhaps a footnote after it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure. I'll try. It would be -- of course we're not referring to the footnote except as a marker, but if you find your footnote 89, the next sentence I believe it says: "The attempts at cooperation were insincere on both sides." And can we correctly understand that to mean that you contend not only that it was the efforts on the Muslim side were insincere but the efforts or the attempts on the HVO side were equally insincere?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the Bosniak Muslim side was much more insincere, as one can see, among other things, from the fact that they sent Colonel Jaganjac and the fact -- and the fact that Mr. Izetbegovic, in his memoirs, does not remember this. But while you're at it, it is interesting to analyse the case of General Praljak here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, my question to you, and if you want to change your report or state a different conclusion to the Chamber you can do so, I suppose, and the Judges will decide, but are you changing your statement? You're saying now that you withdraw the conclusion that these attempts were insincere on both sides?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you tell me once again where that is, because I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After footnote 89, sir, in the text.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot conclude that from my text. Oh, no. Sorry. I've found it. I did not say the amount of insincerity. I said that both sides were insincere and then I proceed to explain why. In the best example of reasons why I think that the Muslims are a little less sincere, that is, a little more insincere, can be found in the text which is quoted above footnote 102. That is throughout the summer of 1992, the BH Army was trying to play the card of Croat armed forces, the HOS, of the Croat party of rights. So I stand by the claim that the Muslims were more insincere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, in fact you've taken us to the next topic, sir. You talked about part of the attempts or however sincere or insincere at Croat-Muslim cooperation at HOS or H-O-S. From your report again, if you can assist us, please, are you saying in your report that HOS was not in fact for an integrated multi-ethnic Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I quoted very clearly the letter of the party's president, Mr. Paraga, to Major Darko Kraljevic, later a member of the HVO. If you want me to, I can read it out to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. In fact, that was once again exactly what I was going to refer you to. Footnote 95 of your paper, on page 31, at least of the English version, footnote 95, in reference to this statement by Mr. Paraga, you say this: "We cannot let the wrong Boban's politics to come back at us. We are absolutely for the unity of Croat people and its common defence. We are likewise for the unity with Muslim people. We shall not retreat from our policy of the integral Bosnia and Herzegovina, in other words, Croatia to the Drina. Any other policy would mean a division of Herceg-Bosna and creation of a new Serbian state this side of Drina, which would be a disaster for both the Croat and the Muslim people." Now again, sir, I'm not sure from your paper. Are you saying that that was not in fact said or are you saying that it was not in fact true? What point are you trying to make about this statement?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to say -- I'm trying to say under A that that is not true, what you have just said; and B, that Mr. Paraga is trying to renew the Independent State of Croatia, which one can see clearly from the sentence which he wrote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're telling the Chamber that the statement we quoted from your report and that I just read to you, that that was false and that was not in fact the bona fide position of HOS? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't know what Mr. Paraga had in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm trying to understand --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm trying to understand, sir, is the position of your paper on this topic, and I do not know if you're drawing into question and saying that this view of HOS is false or do you indeed agree that that was the stated philosophy and programme, if you will, of Mr. Paraga and his party?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Paraga probably really thought this. But I'm telling you that here he means a concept which - how shall I put it? - which will be held against the Croat people as long as there are any Croats living and which damaged most the Croat people in World War II. This is a defeated policy, a policy which was defeated with a large dose of crime, unfortunately. And, sir, HOS, I'm sure you know what HOS looked like visually. And HOS is to this day used to discredit Croatia in the press, especially in Croatia. We always see the same photographs of the same people who had a "U" on their caps. Unfortunately, the HOS wore this symbol of an ugly part of the Croatian past. It is not mine to agree with him or not. I'm saying what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, didn't it true that it wasn't only the HOS members that wore the letter "U" prominently on their caps or uniforms? Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from time to time, now and then I did see a member of the HVO and the Croatian Army here and there who would be wear such -- this emblem, but those were -- such instances were few and far between.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The HOS commander, that you say in the same paragraph of your report, that was killed, you're referring to Blaz Kraljevic who was assassinated in August 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean Darko Kraljevic, subsequently the commander of the Knights of Vitezovi, in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring in your report to where you say in the area of Mostar, HOS was on bad terms with the HVO and close to the BH Army until the death of their commander. And when you're talking about the death of the commander you're referring to the killing of Blaz Kraljevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm referring to Blaz Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges, sir, was he assassinated by forces or persons associated with the HDZ and HVO because he and HOS were seen as a pro-Muslim competitor or threat to the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, I didn't see documents referring to this so that I'd rather not say anything about it. Many guesses, many stories circulate around about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in all your work as an historian that you've told us about, in terms of some of the various key events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you have no views on this topic, the killing of Blaz Kraljevic as commander of the HOS? Is that correct? If that's correct, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecutor spent today, more than an hour, repeating questions from the direct examination, which, too, the Chamber would not allow me to do. When I merely tried to do something like that during my examination. He spent the time in a suspicious attempt to discredit the witness, and he got to the documentation after two hours. So I object and I protest, because the Prosecution examination has taken longer than the direct examination. If the Prosecutor is again allowed to do it, I will consider it unfair to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think, you know, most of the cross-examination is concentrated on the reports which is in our hand, and we Judges also have some problems with the reading of these reports, I think partially because of the translation matters, and partially we are not quite familiar with the situations here. So I don't think there is any problem to ask some questions on the reports. Yes, Mr. Scott. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you know your report, and in the interest of time, I'm not going to read out the entire top third of page 13 of the English version, but in terms of HOS being viewed as a threat or a competitor to the HDZ or the HVO, you cite here, do you not, a report or a communication from Milivoj Petkovic, and you give six, what some people call bullet items, all to the effect, are they not, that Mr. Petkovic was concerned or complaining that the Muslims seemed to be dealing and going to HOS instead of the HVO? Isn't that a fair reading?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can conclude from the report based on what General Petkovic said, that the BH Army did not make any attempts to cooperate with the HVO, which again I put it in one of my footnotes, which some faxes of some documents that General Siber published in his book, in his war diary, that is, dating from 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could it not be that the reason that the Muslims were going to HOS and not the HVO is because they believed that HOS indeed was for a multi-ethnic Bosnia and the HVO was not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you very much. Let us allow the witness to finish his thought. Mr. Prosecutor, my learned friend, is -- keeps interrupting him in the middle of his sentences. He has done it again. I think it would be only fair to the witness to give him an opportunity to finish his thought and to answer the question completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, from the transcript I thought the witness had already finished his answer. But if you're not, please continue your answer of that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. From the text of the report by Mr. Petkovic and from your contention -- actually, I should like to go back to your contention about the HOS as the advocate of the multi-ethnic Bosnia and Herzegovina. I believe that this could not be called that way. We can only talk about the HOS as the advocate of a single state of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the principle of the dual ethnicity or two ethnic principle. So in very simple terms, it would be a multi-ethnic state. The HOS was not at all interested in Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which all of you, the Muslims and the HVO, were fighting at that time; correct? The Serbs. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Although I could use this to remind you of some of your allegations about the limited combat activities of the HVO against Republika Srpska, that is, of its army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's your position, sir, on page 8 of your report, if I understand it correctly, that at least in their public pronouncements, the Muslims spoke in favour of a multi-ethnic Bosnia-Herzegovina with the co-existence of all peoples and joint action with the Croats, the Bosnian Croats, against the Serbs. Page 8 of your report. So do you agree that in fact among the three groups, the three prior -- excuse me, principal groups, that the Muslims were more in favour of multi-ethnic Bosnia than the other two?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please draw my attention to the place where you found this? Maybe you can give me another footnote as the indicator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, for example, right after your footnote 57. You say -- you say -- excuse me, just so we're clear because you've asked me. You said: "According to the directive, the main task was supposed to be the protection of Muslim people, the protection of the territorial integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to secure the future co-existence of all the peoples and nationalities in the state territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I quote the commander of the Patriotic League, Mr. Sefer Halilovic. And further on in the text, I comment upon that. I draw the attention to some illogical points, and I also warn that Mr. Halilovic does something that a professional historian does not find appropriate, i.e. brings an incomplete document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. My question to you now is this, sir: Is it the position -- is it your position, as stated in your report or not, that of the three groups, the Muslims were the most pro-multi-ethnic Bosnia of the three groups? If I misunderstand your report, sir, please correct me.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to this concrete comment that I gave you a little while ago? Then your interpretation is wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do not believe that that was their -- that was the Muslim position. Is that what you're telling us, that perhaps it was stated but not what they meant?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already told you what this is. And somewhat earlier the same person, Halilovic, talked about an extremist wing of the HDZ. Yesterday I admitted that I was not very clear as to what he referred to, and I believe that my work shows it very clearly. One needs to make a distinction between a promotion, although this is not what he does here, because these are combat reports, combat documents. But I believe that you also know it only too well that the BH Army in Sarajevo did not come out very glorious when it came to multi-ethnicity. That started with the year 1992 and the stories about Stup and then ended in 1993, and the activities of certain gentlemen, both by the name of Celo and a third one called Musan Topalovic - Caco.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, getting into a level of detail, sir, I don't want to get too bogged down in. So the way you've corrected me then, is that you admit these are the public statements of the Muslims, but your view is that they were not genuine. Is that what you're trying to tell us?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. If I may, I would like to draw your attention to the methods used in the work of a historian, which is the method that I have used, and it is called the criticism of sources. Historians are very often put into a situation in which they conclude that the proclaimed and what is written in laws and what can be read on papers does not reflect the real life, and that is what this method is all about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you suggesting that governments or political parties or organisations can take one position publicly and actually have a different agenda in private?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: History is full of such examples. It is more of a rule than an exception.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, for instance, when the HDZ or HVO said that they were for a sovereign multi-ethnic Bosnia, they didn't really mean an unitary, ethnically mixed state based on one person, one vote, did they?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: An unitarian Bosnia and Herzegovina is certainly not what they had in mind, but one cannot deny the fact that the HVO, and here I mean the military component of it, was the only warring party which at a certain moment in time had members of another people amongst its ranks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You deny, sir, that there were a number of Croat -- relatively senior Croat officers in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there were two, as far as I know. Stepan Siber was one. And maybe it wouldn't be a bad idea for you to read his memoirs. And as far as I know, there was also a Brigadier Ivan Brigic. As regards Mr. Siber, I have come across his name in several places, and those were from the period of the Yugoslav People's Army. The said person is there referred to as "Stjepan." "Stjepan" is not a Croatian name. He must have remembered only subsequently what his ethnic background was. I would also like to comment upon the case of the second high-ranking officer of the BH Army. That is Mr. Divjak. I said that yesterday, Mr. Izetbegovic, in his memoirs, published his dismissal notice which -- that is, his resignation, which I quoted here. And this shows the character of the multi-ethnicity of the command staff of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was nothing but propaganda. I would most heartily advise you to read that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. There has been a misprint in the transcript which leads to a misunderstanding of the witness's words. Page 59, line 16. The name should be spelled Stepan, S-T-E-P-A-N, without a "J", because Stepan is the name which is not Croatian, as the witness said. When the name is written like this, there is a misunderstanding, because Stepan and Stjepan are two different names. I know this may not mean much to you, but this is what the witness wanted to explain to all of us and this is how the transcript should read. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, do you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is exactly what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So again, just to finish on this point, sir, your position is that in this particular regard that you talked about with Mr. Izetbegovic, that these claims were nothing but propaganda; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. If you want me to read a part of this letter, a part of this resignation, I will gladly do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. You've answered my question, sir. My next question to you is: And wasn't it exactly the same type of propaganda when the HVO denied having any plans to join what they considered the Bosnian Croat parts of Bosnia to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which specific allegations and which time do you have in mind? You seem to be confusing matters a little bit. You seem to be confusing terms. We're now talking about the structure of the officer, personnel, and now you're talking about high politics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you said a few moments ago, and you said words to the effect and the screen has passed but that history is full of examples where various leaders, movements, political parties, said one thing and meant something quite the other. And that can be equally said of the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes, although one needs to insist on specific allegations and on specific period of time. I was very specific a little while ago when I gave you the example of the BH Army, unlike you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can -- well, sir, if we have time, we may get some additional specific examples, I can assure you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask the witness to be shown Defence Exhibits D/72 and D/73 which we did not have the translations of yesterday, and my understanding is that those translations have been made available.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could they be put on the ELMO, please, because the interpreters do not have them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I can ask you, first of all, to look at D2/72. Perhaps we can assist the translation?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't know if it would assist the translation if the English was placed on the ELMO or not. The witness is looking at the B/C/S version presumably.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Either language, as long as we can see the text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Starting with D2/72. Again, sir, and not having had -- not being able to read the document yesterday during your direct examination, for which I apologise, I'm not sure the point that you're trying to make. Are you saying that there are statements or matters in this document that are false, are not accurate?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely do not follow you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you can refresh our memory now that we have the translation, the Judges and I and others have the translation of the document. If you recall, maybe you don't recall, what point you were trying to make by showing us this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I interrupt, please, for a moment? My note, and I found the documents very interesting I must say when they were translated, my note from yesterday is that this witness described them as a core set of documents which caused the war between the Croats and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Judge Clark, that's what I heard as well, and that's why I'm coming back to them, to make sure we understand them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your contention, sir, D2/72 and 73 should be understood by the Judges to provide a core explanation to how the war or why the war started?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still adhere to my yesterday's statement, only I didn't understand you fully. You were talking about the HVO, so I thought that maybe you would bring me an HVO document. I'm going to repeat now what I said to you yesterday. This document is important for two reasons. This document clearly shows on the example of the 4th Corps of the BH Army that the BH Army was continuing to get the supplies of armament and equipment which the HVO, some of it takes, but most of it let's through. That's the first reason. And I think I put it in my remarks. The reason for that was that General Rasim Delic, in his memoirs, claims that between November 1990 -- after November 1992, the flow of arms stopped, whereas Mr. Izetbegovic, in his memoirs, says and mentions even the quantity of weapons and other equipment that arrive in Sarajevo and reach the BH Army. Secondly, the commander of the 4th Corps, I believe that this document was signed by the chief -- his Chief of Staff, asks for certain measures to be put in place in the area of responsibility of his corps, and these measures to be aimed against the HVO. Seven days later, minutes were compiled which confirms that these measures were indeed put in place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me -- just to move us along because we have about a half an hour left this evening. Perhaps we can take both documents then and come back to them as a unit. Let me direct your attention for a moment to the next exhibit then, D2/73. And I'm going to start by asking you the same question that I asked you about the prior document. Is there anything in this document, any assertions, the things that are being reported, which you say are false or not accurately presented in the document?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose there are a number of accurate statements on the first and second page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question to you, sir, having both of those documents now in mind, and I asked you earlier today in my cross-examination, I said are you prepared to give -- is it true that the Muslims had the same rights of organisation and self-defence as the Croat people did, and you said yes. So what do you find objectionable, please, to the Muslims reacting to convoys being stopped, humanitarian aid being stopped, ABiH soldiers being arrested, the issuance of Herceg-Bosna licence plates as an affront to the central government, an HVO tax system put in place, the seizing of flats and businesses? The Muslims had no basis to object to all that? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Muslims had the right to fight against it, except the way in which they did it is somewhat questionable, Mr. Prosecutor. Just a little too many people got killed. Just a little -- there was a little too much fire or a little too much violence. Too many settlements got burnt down. Questionable is also the way in which it was done, and questionable is also -- and these -- and the -- the census is also questionable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- described it pretty accurately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Sometimes the interpretation stops and I think it's finished. I'm not trying to be impolite, Witness. And when you say things were a little bit questionable, a little bit too extreme, you're telling the Judges, are you, that none of that extremism, none of those questionable things happened on the HVO side?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, it is always a question, it is always a matter of the level. HVO outbursts are mostly of the technical nature, and this is the strategic level. Two days later, this document was seized by the HVO. This document was published in March or perhaps early April in a local newspaper of the Konjic HVO. I believe the paper is called Aviza. That is what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that regard, in fact, sir, you say on page 9 of your report, you say that: "the Serbs engaged in ethnic cleansing and concentration camps." And so that we again can speak as much as possible, understanding your terms, when you say ethnic cleansing, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: By this I mean exactly the expulsion, killing of members of a different ethnic origin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say that the Serbs used concentration camps as a means or a tool, as an instrument of ethnic cleansing, what do you mean in saying that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment until I find it. Well, all I said was that the practice of ethnic cleansing had started and establishment of concentration camps. You're interpreting my sentence rather liberally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you didn't mean to suggest that concentration camps was one of the ways that ethic cleansing was carried out. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by "ethnic cleansing," I mean the expulsion of people. A concentration camp is a detention and collection, and there is a different between them. However, the effect is, to all intensive purposes, the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's your position, from your paper, that during the years, the war years, from 1991 to 1995, the Serbs engaged in ethnic cleansing; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's your position that during the war years, from 1991 to 1995, the Serbs used concentration camps as part of their programme; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your position that Muslims engaged in ethnic cleansing during this same time period?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position is that Croats and Muslims and Serbs equally engaged in ethnic cleansing during that time, that is, during the war in individual areas. It all depended on the war in question and the adversary, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 17, you say that concerning -- with a reference to 1993, you say: "The treatment of the civilians," and if it's a problem with translation I apologise but I won't paraphrase, I'll just read the translation of your report as it was given to us. It says: "The treatment of the civilians, such as until then, had been a characteristic of the engagement of the Serb forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were quite often, and those were to become a strong argument for the equalisation of the Croats with the Serbs." Are we to understand that statement that the Croats followed in the footsteps of the Serbs, engaging in similar behaviour?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you tell me the footnote so that I can find the text, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last sentence in the second to last paragraph starting on that page. It's after footnote 148.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm saying here that in the latter half, sometime in May 1993, roughly, the -- the practice of ethnic cleansing begins to emerge among Croats, and the concentration camps emerge, but only as of May 1993, after the beginning of the war against the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Forgive me, Mr. President. I'm looking to see if there are any topics -- I'm looking to see if there are any topics I can complete in approximately 15 minutes. I'm not sure that there is, but we'll just have to go as far as we can and then pick up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true, as stated in your paper again, and one particular example is on page 20, that the Republic of Croatia's President Tudjman's goal and obsession, and obsession is your word so I'm not accused of I can hyperbolic. Tudjman's goal and obsession was the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina and bringing parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina into the Croatian state; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, can you help me with the footnote number?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. It's not immediately following the footnote. It goes on -- it's between footnotes 159 and 160. In the English version it is the last full paragraph on page 20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between paragraph -- excuse me. I'm sorry. Between footnote 159 and footnote 160 in the text you say this: "The views of Franjo Tudjman on Bosnia-Herzegovina were not a secret. He did not believe in its viability, which can be documented by his statements and parenthetically less probable by the claims various witnesses of the history." And specifically when I said you used the word "obsession," you go on to say: "It is not serious to reduce the policy of the Republic of Croatia towards Bosnia-Herzegovina to Tudjman's obsession with a division of Bosnia." And my question to you: That's you position; correct? President Franjo Tudjman was obsessed with the division of Bosnia and joining part of it with Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really admire you, because you obviously keep finding things that I did not write. I did not write that, so obviously the translation is incorrect. All I said -- let's clarify it. That Franjo Tudjman, and that is my opinion, that his point of departure was the idea that Bosnia and Herzegovina could not be sustained, that it could not survive. And I believe that the Dayton Bosnia confirms that view. I'm not sure. At least I did not see. Any documents where he would be speaking about the time and manner of separation of Herceg-Bosna and its annexation to the Republic of Croatia. And that would not be serious. That would be flippant in view -- that would be too facetious in view of the situation in which the Republic of Croatia was in, bearing in mind the existence of the Republic of Serb Krajina. That is what I wanted to say. And this claim of yours I really, however hard I try, I cannot find it here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not say, and we can check the translation, we'll have the B/C/S translators go back and look at your original language, you're telling the Chamber that you did not write about Tudjman's obsession with the division of Bosnia? You're denying that that was your -- those are your words?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will read it, sentence, out to you, and it reads: "It is not serious to reduce -- to bring down the policy of the Republic of Croatia towards BH to Tudjman's obsession with the division of Bosnia." And you're obviously reading something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the point is made, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask the witness to be shown comb PT/1. It should be in the second bundle of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. I saw you are standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my client is feeling very bad. May he be allowed to leave the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, he may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm having placed in front of you and it's in the second larger bundle of documents, Exhibit PT/1. It is a transcript of a meeting in the offices of Franjo Tudjman on the 8th of June 1991, starting at approximately 10.00. And I'm going to refer you specifically to, in the B/C/S version I will try to give you the page --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. When the copying was made, I'm afraid I lost my markings, so I'm going to have to look at it myself in a bit more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my colleague Mrs. Nika Pinter warns me that the translation of the sentence that was quoted by the expert witness is not recorded in the way in which the expert witness read it in Croatian. So perhaps he could do it slower, perhaps once again, so that our interpreters could have time to interpret it properly. My colleagues warns me that this sentence makes no sense the way in which it appears here in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we only have ten minutes left for today. So perhaps the interpreters will check it during the night against the transcript as well as the record, and tomorrow morning we'll come back to that and to see how it is translated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if I can direct your attention in particular to -- if you can find in the B/C/S version -- if you'll look in the upper-left corner, sir, there is a series of numbers. I'm going to use those to try to assist you. If you find 0150-9014. And not that page but perhaps the page in front of it. And for the English readers, I'm referring to page of the translation L0045880. And if you can find this language, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is if it is a document. It is nonetheless an integral text, and I'd consider it necessary, because this witness is not an ordinary witness, I think that it would be necessary for this witness, for your expert witness, to familiarise with him -- himself with the complete text rather than with this fragment only, because if we are to be here for several days, then let's do it for several days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it all depends what kind of question the Prosecutor is going to ask. I understand that this document is a very long document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if I could start, sir, again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You can draw the attention to the first page of the document and lay some background to the document and later on put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a document that has been admitted into evidence by the Chamber. The full document, of course, is in the record. I tried to save at least one branch -- one small branch of a tree by not copying the entire document yet again. Obviously the Defence has the entire document, both the original B/C/S version and the translation. I can certainly make it available, with the Court's permission, this could make it available to -- that particular document available to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think that what the President is suggesting to you and indeed what Mr. Seric is saying is that this witness doesn't know what happened before. So in fairness to the witness, you should tell him what the document is or what you say that it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Clark. I did not appreciate that was the point, and I thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, so you know the document we're referring to, a number of documents have come into evidence in this case that were provided by the government of the Republic of Croatia, of records of meetings in the offices of the president, President Tudjman, dating from, roughly speaking, 1991 into 1993 and 1994, perhaps a few later. These are transcripts made from recordings, and they have been used and shown to a number of witnesses in the course of the trial. So what I'm trying to show you now, put before you and ask you questions about, are statements attributed to President Tudjman during a meeting on the 8th of June, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a free interpretation of the Prosecutor concerning these documents. The Defence says "allegedly." These are allegedly the presidential transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your statement is registered in the transcript. You may proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I directed you a few moments ago to 0 -- in the B/C/S version 0150-9014. And if you can perhaps go back about ten or 15 lines before you get to that page, this is the language, part of the language, I'd like to direct your attention to, please. It's the language which says: "So this is the reality that we cannot overlook. Also, gentlemen, if we opt for Croatia's independence, either within an alliance or total independence, Croatia's borders, such as they are today, are absurd. They are impossible in the sense of administration and trade let alone as regards any kind of protection of these borders of Croatia." And if I could ask you then to go to -- if you can find page 01 -- I will ask a question, trying to do this as quickly as possible, at 0150-9047. And for the English -- the translation starts another page 1, but translation page in the upper right corner is L0042599.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in this case, the original is the Croatian text, not the English translation which Mr. Scott has been reading to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's true, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not objecting to you, interpreters, because you're interpreting or, rather, you are saying what Mr. Scott was reading from the English translation and then saying in this case I am saying this for reasons of procedure, because we're dealing about the procedure, not interpretation. The original is the Croatian text, and the -- and our expert witness has this original with him. So the Prosecutor is making a mistake when he's reading the English version as the original and giving us the transcript, which sounds like but not exactly as what the Croatian original says. Since we have the expert witness here, he knows English, let us have him read out what is in the original. What Mr. Scott has said does not correspond with the Croatian original. So we're talking about the Croatian original, not the English original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think this document has been admitted into evidence already. If you have some problems with the translation, you may raise it. It will help us, you know, to arrive at the correct conclusion. Well, Mr. Scott, I really hope you could finish, you know, this part of the cross-examination. So we may sit a little bit longer. You may ask the witness to read the certain corresponding paragraph in his language. Let's see the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I would be happy to. Of course it's only too true that I can only read the document and put my questions in English. I apologise for that. I directed the witness to, in the B/C/S document, 0150-9047. And on that page, we contend, he can read it and tell me if he thinks it's wrong, that on that page -- the middle of the page is the word "president," which I think he can see, "predsednik," and in that paragraph, toward the end of the paragraph it says: "Therefore, the solution lies in what is said there, in the partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And if he achieve that, we can look for a basis of alliance of sovereign republics and states." And all this, sir, is simply to go, given your statement that it was President Tudjman's obsession, the division of Bosnia, wouldn't surprise you, would it, to see him make such statements?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that his obsession was the division of Bosnia. And please listen to what I'm saying. But what you are now saying, I can't find it. I cannot find it. I don't know where you've --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps if I can be shown the document --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- taken that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps if the Chamber gives me the document I can point it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we do not have those numbers on the transcript. They have all been cut off. All we can see is 0509. We cannot see 47. So I don't not have them and the witness does not have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's come back to the report. I think that paragraph is after the footnotes 159.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That's the part where we got into this whole issue some time ago now about Tudjman's obsession, which the witness then read to us and used -- well, he says -- at least as translated exactly that word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's do it again. Let's do it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm referring to your reports. The sentence occurs between footnote 159 and footnote 160 which there is some number of lines of text between the two footnotes. On the English version, and I say that for the benefit of the Judges and others, it's on the bottom of page 20. And you say: "It is not serious to reduce the policy of the Republic of Croatia towards BH to Tudjman's obsession with the division of Bosnia." Now, did you write that or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness -- Witness -- Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you find that sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please read it in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "It is not serious to bring down the policy of the Republic of Croatia towards BH or to restrict the Republic of Croatia to BH to Tudjman's obsession with the division of Bosnia." I'd like to comment. It seems my impression is that the Prosecutor does not understand the sentence, or, rather, that he reads it as he pleases. I believe I've already said it somewhere, briefly commented. The circles which without proper argument talk about this -- well, let me use the Prosecutor's expression, obsession, Tudjman's obsession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me correct you, sir. You've now said it several times. That's your word, not mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, allow the witness to explain to the end, because these are linguistic matters, and the witness is right, the Prosecutor does not understand. What the Prosecutor is saying is not what the witness is saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's not the Prosecutor's expression "obsession." Let's pass this. You may continue, Witness. You may continue, Witness. We don't have much time. We have to stop very soon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain this? I'm saying here that it is not serious to name the policy of the Republic of Croatia as "Tudjman's obsession with the division of Bosnia." The Prosecutor cuts off the first part of the sentence, pulls it out of the context, and then dangles it in front of my nose. I have never experienced anything like that before. And perhaps it wouldn't be bad if he read the rest of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've read that statement now a number of times. It's been translate add number of times. The point is made, I submit, and the only question that was pending before all this started again was:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on what you see attributed, the statements you see in Exhibit PT1 attributed to President Franjo Tudjman doesn't surprise you, do they, given what you describe as Tudjman's obsession with the division of Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I'm telling you nicely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Mr. President, but let us conclude that once and for all. The Prosecutor keeps insisting on something that the witness did not say and did not write. He keeps insisting on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we could not get the meaning of what the witness said. Let the witness tell us what does it mean, the whole sentence. Yes, Witness, you may tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, right. I'll try to explain this sentence. I mean that the policy of the Republic of Croatia is reduced or, rather, that certain circles called the policy of the Republic of Croatia towards Bosnia-Herzegovina "Tudjman's obsession with the division of Bosnia," and I am saying clearly that this is a construct. I merely say that that is what this policy is called. I'm not claiming that. I do not understand how the Prosecutor can draw such conclusions, and I do not understand how is it in these pages that have been shown to me from this record I did not see those sentences. And I know the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that we still get nowhere. Are you going to pursue this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That particular line of questioning --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology. Not specifically, Mr. President. I'm not finished on the topic of in fact the Croatian state policy and what was happening there, but on that particular set of evidence, I don't think anything more productive can come of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. So could we stop here and resume tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you still remember what I told you yesterday afternoon, that you are still under oath. So do not talk to anybody and do not let anybody talk to you about your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Have a good rest and be prepared for tomorrow. We will rise until tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
